etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English furet, ferret, from Old French furet, from Vulgar Latin *furittum (“weasel, ferret”), diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”).
senses: A long-bodied domesticated mammal of the species Mustela furo, descended from the European polecat and often trained to hunt burrowing animals.
(by extension, ambitransitive) To uncover and bring to light by searching; usually to ferret out.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
senses: (dated) A tape of silk, cotton, or ribbon, used to tie documents, clothing, etc. or along the edge of fabric.
